claims.text: A hybrid defect-aware simulation approach will predict electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical models in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The modeled bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains natural lattice defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework couples molecular dynamics and machine learning and explicitly represents realistic defect distributions, including oxygen.
The framework adjusts electron–phonon and impurity-scattering parameters rather than assuming perfect crystallinity.
Oxygen impurities induce lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Ionized-impurity scattering dominates electrical transport in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Enhanced lattice vibrations and thermally activated scattering are important in HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Defects and oxygen precipitates foster local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect-associated local structure mediates carrier scattering and modifies the phonon density of states.
Explicitly modeling defect-induced scattering and anharmonic phonon interactions addresses shortcomings of conventional analytical models.
At low temperature, oxygen-impurity scattering reduces carrier mobility in HfNbTaTiZr.
At high temperature, defect-mediated vibrational changes and lattice expansion alter electron–phonon interactions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The hybrid approach will better match measured activation energies and absolute conductivity values in both temperature regimes.
Including impurity scattering will increase predicted resistivity in the 0–200 K regime.
The model will capture a crossover to phonon-dominated conduction with increased lattice anharmonicity in the 300–1200 K regime.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions underestimate carrier scattering and therefore overpredict conductivity, especially at low temperature.
The approach is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with similar defect structures and oxygen content and requires adjustment for other compositions, pressures, or impurity levels.
Prediction accuracy may depend sensitively on the parameterization of defect scattering.
